text: Every quantum computing result you'll produce in this course, a measurement histogram, a Bloch sphere, a convergence curve, eventually has to become a picture someone can actually read. This lesson covers the Matplotlib building blocks you'll reuse in every visualization lesson that follows.

Modern Matplotlib code almost always starts by creating a Figure, the overall canvas you save, and one or more Axes, the specific surface you call plot and set_xlabel on. An unlabeled plot is a decoration, not a scientific plot, so always set a title, both axis labels, and a legend when there's more than one series. Color alone isn't always enough to distinguish curves, so linestyle and markers matter too. And plt dot subplots returns a grid of axes in one call for laying out related plots side by side.

label equals on each plot call feeds ax dot legend, without a label a series shows up in the plot but not in the legend. This two-line waveform comparison, cosine and sine, gets a title, an x-axis label, and a legend built automatically from those two label arguments.

plt dot subplots of one row and two columns returns a figure and an array of two axes in one call. With a single row, axes is indexed directly, axes zero and axes one, each getting its own title. fig dot tight_layout automatically adjusts spacing so titles and labels on neighboring panels don't overlap.
Next lesson turns amplitudes into the single most common plot you'll produce for the rest of this course: a bar chart of measurement probabilities.
